b1: Low selectivity means it also blocks β2 in the airways, which can tighten them, a big problem for people with asthma.
Too much β1 block slows the heart (bradycardia) and can make people tired.

antagonist: All β-blockers end in -olol (metoprolol, atenolol, propranolol).

b2: Low selectivity also activates β1 in the heart, causing palpitations and a fast heart rate.
Strong β2 activation makes skeletal muscle tremble and pushes potassium into cells.

agonist: β2 agonists end in -terol (albuterol, salmeterol, formoterol).

a1: Off-target hits on other adrenergic receptors in vessels.
Too much α1 block drops blood pressure when standing (orthostatic hypotension).
a2: Off-target hits on other receptors in salivary glands.
Sleepiness, rebound high BP if stopped
Strong α2 activation sedates; stopping suddenly causes a blood pressure rebound.

agonist: Central α2 agonists end in -onidine (clonidine, moxonidine).

m: Blocking muscarinic receptors everywhere dries secretions and slows the gut ("can't see, can't pee, can't spit").
Strong muscarinic block can stop the bladder emptying.

antagonist: Inhaled antimuscarinics end in -tropium (ipratropium, tiotropium); the charged N keeps them out of the brain.

ache: Extra acetylcholine at the heart's muscarinic receptors slows it.
Too much acetylcholine overstimulates the gut and glands (cholinergic effects).

inhibitor: Many cholinesterase inhibitors end in -stigmine (pyridostigmine, rivastigmine).

mu: Off-target histamine release from mast cells.
μ receptors in the brainstem breathing centre and the gut: too much activation slows breathing and stops the bowel.

agonist: Opioid names don't share one stem, so pick any name you like.

d2: Off-target hits on histamine H1 and serotonin receptors.
D2 block in the striatum causes Parkinson-like stiffness; D2 activation triggers the vomiting centre.

agonist: No official stem; -pexole is a nod to pramipexole.

ht3: Blocking gut serotonin signalling slows the bowel.
ht1: 5-HT1B receptors in heart arteries narrow too, so these are avoided in heart disease.

agonist: Migraine drugs of this class end in -triptan (sumatriptan).

cgrp: Off-target effect on gut CGRP signalling.

antagonist: Small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonists end in -gepant (rimegepant, ubrogepant).

h1: Low selectivity hits muscarinic receptors (old antihistamines).

h2: Very low acid can let gut bacteria overgrow.
gaba: Off-target GABA-A subtypes in the spinal cord.
pp: Very strong acid suppression for years.
cox: Unselective COX-1 block removes stomach-protecting prostaglandins.

inhibitor: Ibuprofen-type NSAIDs end in -profen; COX-2-selective ones in -coxib.

ace: ACE also breaks down bradykinin; extra bradykinin irritates the airways.

ins: Too much insulin action drops glucose: shaky, sweaty, confused.

agonist: Insulins don't follow one stem; this is just a nod to insulin.

dpp4: Only when combined with other glucose-lowering drugs.
sglt2: More glucose and water lost in the urine.
sert: Extra serotonin in the gut and brain early on.

inhibitor: Several reuptake inhibitors end in -oxetine (fluoxetine, duloxetine).

nkcc: The same transporter family in the inner ear.
Too much salt and water lost in urine.

inhibitor: Loop diuretics often end in -semide (furosemide, torasemide).

hmg: Statins can affect muscle cell energy.

vkor: Too little clotting: bruising, nosebleeds, worse.

inhibitor: Warfarin-type drugs are coumarins; no single modern stem.

nmda: Off-target hits on other glutamate receptors.

antagonist: Nod to memantine; no official stem.

naka: The pump is in many tissues.

ca: Dilating small arteries but not veins pushes fluid into the ankles.

blocker: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers end in -dipine (amlodipine).

na: Sodium channels in the cerebellum and eye-movement pathways.

blocker: A family of anti-seizure sodium channel blockers ends in -carbazepine.

xo: Rapid uric acid shifts can trigger a flare.

inhibitor: Many enzyme inhibitors end in -stat; febuxostat is an -ostat.

cyslt: Reported with this class; monitored in trials.
maob: Too much dopamine effect: twitchy movements
rib: Some of these also stimulate gut motility.

gyr: Class effect on heart potassium channels.

at1: Blocks angiotensin II at its receptor.

ht1: Narrows dilated head vessels and calms trigeminal nerve endings.

cox: Cuts prostaglandin pain signalling; helps milder attacks.

diseases.name: Epilepsy (focal seizures)
diseases.end: seizures cut by half or more

na: Stops neurons firing in rapid bursts, so seizures can't spread.
nmda: Less excitatory glutamate, but side effects limit it.

gaba: Blocking GABA-A removes the brain's brake: it can CAUSE seizures.

diseases.name: Asthma
diseases.end: fewer attacks and better breathing tests

h1: Histamine is only a small player in asthma.

b2: Blocking β2 TIGHTENS the airways: an asthma attack.
b1: β-blockers can spill over onto β2 and worsen asthma.

glp1: More insulin when sugar is high, less glucagon, slower stomach, less appetite.
sglt2: Kidneys dump extra glucose into the urine; also protects heart and kidneys.
dpp4: Lets the body's own GLP-1 last longer.
ins: Directly lowers glucose but risks hypoglycemia.

d2: Stands in for the missing dopamine in the striatum.
maob: Slows dopamine breakdown in the brain.

sert: More serotonin in synapses; effects build over weeks as the brain adapts.
nmda: Fast-acting antidepressant effect via glutamate signalling.
maob: MAO-B mainly handles dopamine, so it's weak for depression.

pbp: Breaks the bacterial cell wall, so the bacteria burst.
rib: Stops bacterial protein making; also covers atypical bacteria.

pp: Switches off the final acid pump.
h2: Blocks histamine's signal to make acid.

diseases.name: Gout prevention
diseases.end: uric acid below target, fewer flares

xo: Less uric acid made, so crystals dissolve over time.
cox: Treats flare pain but doesn't lower uric acid.

hmg: Liver makes less cholesterol and pulls LDL from blood.

b1: Protects the heart from constant adrenaline (start low, go slow).
naka: Stronger squeeze, but a narrow safety margin.

b1: Whipping a failing heart harder worsens it long-term.

vkor: Fewer working clotting factors; needs blood tests.
cox: Antiplatelet effect is too weak for AF clots.

h1: Blocks histamine's itch, sneeze and runny nose.
a1: Shrinks swollen nose vessels (decongestant) but raises BP.

ht3: Blocks serotonin from damaged gut cells reaching the vomiting centre.
nk1: Blocks substance P in the vomiting centre (needs to reach the brain).
d2: Blocks dopamine in the vomiting trigger zone.

ache: More acetylcholine for the surviving memory neurons (modest help).

m: Anticholinergic drugs WORSEN memory and confusion.

ache: More acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction to outcompete the antibodies.
s1p: Immune modulation helps some autoimmune diseases, but isn't standard here.

d2: Blocks excess dopamine signalling in the limbic pathway.

d2: More dopamine signalling can WORSEN psychosis.

mu: Strongest pain relief by turning down pain signals in brain and spinal cord.
na: Local nerve block numbs the area.

tpo: Stops the thyroid making new hormone.
b1: Calms the racing heart and tremor but doesn't fix the hormone.

s1p: Traps lymphocytes in lymph nodes so fewer reach the brain and attack myelin.

pp: Less acid lets the ulcer heal.

cox: NSAIDs CAUSE ulcers by removing stomach-protecting prostaglandins.
